title: Performative Policy Gradient: Optimality in Performative Reinforcement Learning
claim: A stability-seeking baseline plateaus early at a suboptimal level, while our method recovers from an initial dip to higher final performance.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, left-to-right over iterations, shaded variance band
description: A single line chart with iteration (0 to 500) on the x-axis and average utility (about 0.10 to 0.16) on the y-axis. A red line for ERM starts with a sharp spike near 0.16, drops almost immediately to about 0.13, and stays flat for the rest of training. A green line for Performatively Optimal also starts high, then falls to about 0.105. It climbs steadily, crosses the red line around iteration 40, and levels off near 0.155. A pale green shaded band shows run-to-run variability. It is widest early on and narrows later, with a small dip near iteration 250. A boxed legend sits in the lower right. The eye goes first to the green curve overtaking the flat red baseline. Gridlines are light and there is no other annotation.
caption: Average utility (over 20 runs) obtained by ERM and Performatively Optimal policies for β = 0.5. of RL assumes the underlying environment to be static, and the goal of RL algorithms is to find a utility-maximising, aka optimal policy, for choosing actions over time. But the static environment assumption does not hold universally.
abstract: Post-deployment machine learning algorithms often influence the environments they act in, and thus shift the underlying dynamics that the standard reinforcement learning (RL) methods ignore. While designing optimal algorithms in this performative setting has recently been studied in supervised learning, the RL counterpart remains under-explored. In this paper, we prove the performative counterparts of the performance difference lemma and the policy gradient theorem in RL, and further introduce the Performative Policy Gradient algorithm (PePG). PePG is the first policy gradient algorithm designed to account for performativity in RL. Under softmax parametrisation, and also with and without entropy regularisation, we prove that PePG converges to performatively optimal policies, i.e. policies that remain optimal under the distribution shifts induced by themselves. Thus, PePG significantly extends the prior works in Performative RL that achieves performative stability but not optimality. Furthermore, our empirical analysis on standard performative RL environments validate that PePG outperforms the existing performative RL algorithms aiming for stability.
